question.prompt:
How many positive integers \(n\) satisfy \[\dfrac{n+1000}{70} = \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor?\]

(Recall that \(\lfloor x\rfloor\) is the greatest integer not exceeding \(x.\))

solutions.title: Use the floor value as a variable
solutions.explanation:
The floor value is an integer, so using it as the variable turns the equation into exact bounds between consecutive squares.

Let \(k=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\). The given equation gives
\[
n=70k-1000.
\]
The definition of the floor function is equivalent to
\[
k^2\le n<(k+1)^2.
\]
Substituting for \(n\), the lower bound becomes
\[
\begin{aligned}
k^2&\le70k-1000,\\
k^2-70k+1000&\le0,\\
(k-35)^2&\le225.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(20\le k\le50\).

The strict upper bound becomes
\[
\begin{aligned}
70k-1000&<(k+1)^2,\\
k^2-68k+1001&>0,\\
(k-34)^2&>155.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(k-34\) is an integer and
\[
12^2=144<155<169=13^2,
\]
its absolute value must be at least \(13\). Therefore \(k\le21\) or \(k\ge47\).

Combining the bounds gives exactly
\[
k=20,21,47,48,49,50.
\]
These produce
\[
n=400,470,2290,2360,2430,2500.
\]
All are positive, and the bounds used are equivalent to the floor condition, so all six work. Different values of \(k\) give different values of \(n\) through \(n=70k-1000\).

There are \(\boxed{6}\) solutions, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

solutions.title: Bound the gap above a square
solutions.explanation:
If \(k=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\), then \(n\) lies only a limited distance above \(k^2\). Bounding this gap lets us eliminate a whole middle range and check a short list.

Write
\[
n=k^2+t,
\]
where \(k\) and \(t\) are integers. Since the next square is \((k+1)^2=k^2+2k+1\), the floor condition is exactly
\[
0\le t\le2k.
\]
The original equation now gives
\[
k^2+t+1000=70k,
\]
so
\[
t=70k-1000-k^2=(k-20)(50-k).
\]
For \(k<20\) or \(k>50\), this product is negative. Hence \(20\le k\le50\), and therefore \(t\le2k\le100\).

We can rule out every \(k\) from \(24\) through \(46\) at once. Write \(k=24+u\), where \(0\le u\le22\). Then
\[
t=(4+u)(26-u)=104+u(22-u)\ge104,
\]
contradicting \(t\le100\).

Only eight values remain. The table compares the required gap \(t=(k-20)(50-k)\) with its allowed maximum \(2k\).

| \(k\) | Required \(t\) | Maximum \(2k\) | Valid? |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| \(20\) | \(0\) | \(40\) | Yes |
| \(21\) | \(29\) | \(42\) | Yes |
| \(22\) | \(56\) | \(44\) | No |
| \(23\) | \(81\) | \(46\) | No |
| \(47\) | \(81\) | \(94\) | Yes |
| \(48\) | \(56\) | \(96\) | Yes |
| \(49\) | \(29\) | \(98\) | Yes |
| \(50\) | \(0\) | \(100\) | Yes |

Thus six values of \(k\) satisfy the exact gap condition. Each gives one positive integer \(n=70k-1000\), and these integers are distinct. All other values of \(k\) have been excluded.

The number of solutions is \(\boxed{6}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
